inline.s: This is called the upper-grade, lower-birth one.
Ren 2: Summary of the name of this contemplation.
This is called the higher-grade rebirth-contemplation; it is the fourteenth contemplation.”

blocks.text: Xin 2: Contemplating the Śrāvaka assembly (the fifteenth, the middle-grade rebirth contemplation) — in two parts

inline.s: The Ling-zhi Commentary says: “The fifteenth covers the three grades of the middle class, and this gathers in the Śrāvaka assembly of the four fruits. The Sūtra says: ‘That Buddha has immeasurable and boundless Śrāvaka disciples, all of them Arhats,’ and so on. Question: That land is a pure Mahāyāna assembly of good companions; how then can there be Śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle? Answer: The Śrāvakas of this world are of two kinds. First, the ‘fixed nature,’ meaning those who sink into emptiness, cling to stillness, and take the path of final nirvāṇa; the Treatise on Rebirth says ‘the two-vehicle seeds are not born there,’ and these belong to that kind. Second, the ‘unfixed nature,’ meaning those who, in between, turn their minds back and, having already been revealed, know the eternal and receive the prophecy. Though they are Śrāvakas, they do not stop at the lesser fruition. In the Lotus these are the ‘true Arhats’; in the Nirvāṇa, the ‘bodhisattvas who have left home.’ The Śrāvakas of the Pure Land are of this same kind. Having heard the great teaching and aroused the bodhi-mind, they at first studied the Lesser Vehicle; hearing of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, they stirred up their old habits and first realized the lesser fruition, but in the end they return to the Great Vehicle. Among these three grades, the upper-birth one always upholds the five, eight, ten, and full precepts — these four kinds of precept practice; the middle-birth one also upholds the four precepts, but only for one day and one night; the lower-birth one is filial, nurturing, and compassionate. The upper two exclusively uphold the Buddha’s precepts and also have the dedication of merit and the seeking of vows. The lowest relies only on worldly teaching, and so meets a good friend only at the end of life. Because the practices of the three stages differ, they are distinguished as high and low.”
First, the middle-grade upper-birth
second, the middle-grade middle-birth; third, the middle-grade lower-birth
Gui 1: The middle-grade upper-birth

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “The upper-birth of the middle grade: If there are sentient beings who uphold the five precepts, observe the eight-precept fast, cultivate the various precepts, commit none of the five grave offenses, and have no faults or misdeeds — with these roots of goodness they dedicate [their merit] and vow to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

First, clarifying the cause of practice. The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘The five and the eight are the precepts of the two assemblies of lay people. The ‘various precepts’ include the ten and the full precepts, the precepts of the five assemblies of renouncers. The five precepts are: first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to commit sexual misconduct; fourth, not to speak falsely; fifth, not to drink alcohol. To the eight precepts three more are added: sixth, not to wear garlands and necklaces, nor anoint the body with fragrant oils; seventh, not to sit on a high [and luxurious] bed, nor sing, dance, or [be entertained by] musicians and singers; eighth, not to eat beyond the midday meal. In the matter of sexual conduct the practice severs both the illicit and the proper, and so it is added as the ‘pure conduct.’ Because it unifies the mind, it is called the ‘eight fasts’; because it confines the faculties, it is also called the ‘eight gates.’ The details are in the vinaya. Moreover, these four kinds of precepts are either upheld separately by the monastic and the lay, or observed together [by those who have gone forth]. Since one upholds the pure precepts, one must depart from all faults. The five grave offenses are the greatest among faults, hence they are singled out. What follows sets forth the dedication of merit and the seeking of vows. The roots of goodness are the cause; being born there is the fruit.’

At the moment of death, Amitabha Buddha, surrounded by an assembly of bhikṣus as his retinue, radiates golden light and comes to where that person is, preaching of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and praising the renunciation of home-life as the means to be freed from all suffering. Seeing this, the practitioner’s heart is filled with great joy. He sees his own body seated upon a lotus throne. Kneeling long with palms joined, he does reverence to the Buddha. Before he has even raised his head, he is reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The lotus opens at once. When the flower unfolds, he hears a multitude of voices praising the Four Noble Truths. In that very moment he attains the Arhat way: the three insights, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations are all complete. This is the upper-birth of the middle grade.

Next, clarifying the experienced fruit. The Yanyi commentary says: ‘The upper three all speak of the Buddha and of the bodhisattvas. That here it speaks only of the Buddha and the bhikṣus is because the transformation [assembly] is of fellow practitioners, drawing in those of the same kind. This is because they at first practiced the lesser practice, and so what is preached to them is likewise only the method of the four foundations of mindfulness.’ The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘Praising the renunciation of home-life makes clear that this grade largely gathers in the monastic assembly. “Freed from suffering” means that in what is near one departs from the entanglements of the dusty world, and in what is far one clears away the afflictions.’ Below ‘the practitioner’ clarifies the rebirth. The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘Seated on the lotus and doing reverence to the Buddha, the consciousness-body is released at once.’ Below ‘the lotus opens’ [clarifies] the benefits after rebirth. The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘(When the lotus opens) there is in fact the vision of the Buddha, but the text omits this and does not make it explicit.’ The Yanyi commentary says: ‘In this grade the flower opens and the Buddha is seen, swifter than the upper-middle and the upper-lower grades. The upper-middle [birth] takes a night, and the upper-lower takes a day and a night before the flower opens. Here it opens at once, not so much as passing a single night. The difference is only in the form of the Buddha seen.’ The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘The praise of the Four Noble Truths accords with what they were accustomed to practice. The two truths of suffering and origin are the worldly cause and effect, and are what is to be abandoned; the two truths of cessation and the path are the transcendent cause and effect, and are what is to be realized. All four dharmas are true, and so they are jointly called truths.’

Below ‘in that very moment’ clarifies the attainment of the way. The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘“A” renders [the Sanskrit] as “not,” and “lo-han” (Arhat) as “born.” When the bonds of defilement are entirely exhausted and one no longer receives a future existence, it is therefore called “not-born.” It is also called “worthy of offerings” and “destroyer of thieves,” as explained elsewhere. The three insights are: the insight [into] past lives, the insight into the extinction of defilements in the present, and the insight into the heavenly eye [of the future]. All three see through to the depths, so alone are they called “insights.” The six supernormal powers are: first, the heavenly eye; second, the heavenly ear; third, knowledge of others’ minds; fourth, knowledge of past lives; fifth, psychic power; sixth, the extinction of defilements. All six are unobstructed, hence they are jointly called “powers.” The eight liberations are also called the “eight abandons.” First, having form within while contemplating forms without — without destroying the inner bone-body, one contemplates the impurity of the outer forms; this stage is in the first dhyāna. Second, not having form within while contemplating forms without — destroying the inner skeleton, one contemplates the outer impurity and enters the second dhyāna. Third, the liberation of the ‘pure object’ realized with the body — setting aside external impurity, the concentrated mind is pure and clear, hence called ‘pure object’; with a detached mind one receives the bliss of the third dhyāna, hence called ‘realized with the body.’ Fourth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite space — extinguishing the forms of the fourth dhyāna, the mind rests on boundless space and enters concentration; knowing impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, the mind is weary and turns away. Fifth, the liberation of the sphere of consciousness — renouncing space and resting on consciousness, one enters concentration; knowing impermanence, one gives rise to weariness and turning away. Sixth, the liberation of the sphere of nothingness — renouncing consciousness and resting on nothingness, one enters concentration; knowing impermanence, one gives rise to weariness and turning away. Seventh, the liberation of ‘neither having perception nor not having perception’ — renouncing nothingness and resting on neither having nor not having, one enters concentration; knowing impermanence, one gives rise to weariness and turning away. Eighth, the liberation of the cessation of feeling and perception — turning away from and extinguishing feeling, renouncing all the mind and mental-factor dharmas, one enters concentration and rests; hence it is called ‘abandon.’ The rest are as set out in the Sequence of the Dharma-Realm.’
Gui 2: The middle-grade middle-birth

The middle-birth of the middle grade: If there are sentient beings who, for one day and one night, observe the eight-precept fast; or for one day and one night observe the novice’s precepts; or for one day and one night observe the full precepts, and their deportment is without any deficiency — with these merits they dedicate [them] and vow to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, cultivated and perfumed by the fragrance of the precepts.

First, the cause of practice. The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘The text here omits the five precepts; earlier it omitted the ten and the full precepts. The two appear alternately, so the four precepts are necessarily complete. The novice’s precepts are the ten precepts. In the earlier eight precepts, the first seven are divided into two [groups], and to them is added “not to grasp gold, silver, and precious things.” The full precepts are the precepts received by the great monks and the great nuns. The seven limbs [of body and speech] are fully aroused and extend everywhere throughout the sphere of living beings, hence they are called “full.” Observing the precepts is a pure karmic practice, undertaken for a pure retribution. Upholding the precepts accomplishes virtue, and the name is heard far and wide, hence it is likened to fragrance.’

For such a practitioner, when his life is about to end, he sees Amitabha Buddha, with his retinue, radiating golden light and holding a lotus of the seven jewels, coming before him. The practitioner himself hears a voice in the sky praising him: ‘Good man! Because you, a good person, have followed the teaching of the Buddhas of the three times, I have come to welcome you!’ The practitioner sees himself seated upon the lotus. The lotus closes at once, and he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. In the jeweled pond, after seven days, the lotus unfolds. Once the flower has opened, he opens his eyes and joins his palms, praising the World-Honored One. Hearing the Dharma, he rejoices and attains Sotāpanna (stream-entry). After half a kalpa he becomes an Arhat. This is the middle-birth of the middle grade.

Next, the experienced fruit. First, the experienced condition. The Buddhas of the three times all encourage the upholding of precepts, the abandoning of evil, and the cultivation of good, so to uphold precepts now is to follow along with them. Next, the rebirth. The lotus closes and one is born — this too is within a single thought-moment. Third, the benefits after rebirth. First, seeing the Buddha. The text narrates the praise [of the Buddha]; accordingly the seeing [of the Buddha] must come first. Next, hearing the Dharma. This too is [the teaching of] the Four Noble Truths — suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and so on. The lower grade is likewise. Third, the realization of the fruit. ‘Sotāpanna’ is here rendered ‘countering the stream’ — that is, countering the stream of birth-and-death; it is the first fruit. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)
Gui 3: The middle-grade lower-birth

The lower-birth of the middle grade: If there are good men and good women who are filial to and support their parents and practice kindness in the world, then when this person’s life is about to end he meets a good spiritual friend, who explains at length to him the joyful things of the land of Amitabha Buddha and also speaks of the forty-eight great vows of the bhikṣu Dharmākara. Having heard these things, he immediately passes away. Just as a mighty warrior bends and extends his arm, in that instant he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. After seven days he meets Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta; hearing the Dharma, he rejoices and attains Sotāpanna. After one small kalpa he becomes an Arhat. This is the lower-birth of the middle grade.

First, the cause of practice. To do labor and serve, to comply with [one’s parents’] countenance and support their aspirations — this is why it is called ‘filially nourishing one’s parents.’ Confucianism regards this as the root of the hundred conduct. Extending love to all beings and giving broadly to succor the many — hence it is called ‘practicing kindness in the world.’ The Confucian tradition regards this as the virtue of the gentleman. Because in life one accumulated goodness, therefore at death one meets the [good] condition. Below ‘this person’ [comes] second, meeting the condition. To transform others through goodness — this is what the many ‘know and recognize’: knowing his virtue, recognizing his appearance. The Lotus Sūtra, the chapter on King Wonderful-Adornment, says: ‘A good spiritual friend is a great sustaining condition’; it points to wife and children as a good spiritual friend. Therefore one knows that so long as one can guide [others], one is not restricted to the monastic or the lay. The joyful things of the land are as the dependent retribution described above and as stated in the Larger and the Smaller Sūtras of Amitāyus. The bhikṣu Dharmākara is the former name of Amitabha in [the time of] his practicing [the path]. Formerly a king, he met the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, renounced his kingdom, and went forth from home; right before the Buddha he made the forty-eight vows. The details are as in the Larger Sūtra. Third, below ‘having heard these things’ [comes] the gaining of rebirth. Here there should be such events as, at death, holding the lotus and welcoming [the practitioner], but the text abbreviates and does not narrate them. ‘As a mighty warrior bends and extends his arm’ is also only a brief moment; the wording before and after varies. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.) The Yanyi commentary says: ‘The two lines below “having heard” precisely set forth that the mind aroused at the end of life is fierce and keen, and so he immediately passes away. At the very moment of death in this world is exactly the time of rebirth in that land. The simile of the mighty warrior’s extending his arm shows the swiftness of that rebirth: dying here and being born there, without passing through the intermediate state, is like the mighty warrior’s bending and extending his arm. That the lotus is not mentioned is because it can be inferred by analogy — the three grades below all have a lotus; how could this grade have none? There is no such case. Fourth, below ‘after seven days’ clarifies the later benefits. In the preceding grade, after seven days the lotus unfolded; here it says ‘after seven days,’ which is somewhat later in time. It certainly will not reach fourteen days for the flower to open. Previously it said ‘praising the World-Honored One, hearing the Dharma and rejoicing’ — that was hearing the Buddha preach; here he meets the two great bodhisattvas preaching. Previously he passed half a kalpa; here he passes one small kalpa. This shows that the earlier ‘half a kalpa’ is also a small kalpa. That the present [grade] is inferior to the former is logically so.’
This is called the middle-class-rebirth contemplation; it is the fifteenth contemplation.”

blocks.text: Xin 3: Contemplating the assembly of the people (the sixteenth, the lower-grade rebirth contemplation) — in two parts

inline.s: First, the lower-grade upper-birth
second, the lower-grade middle-birth; third, the lower-grade lower-birth

The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘The three grades of the lower class all have no cause of cultivation; they are all people who did evil throughout their lives and meet a good [friend] at the end of life. According to the Ten Doubts Treatise, if there were no good roots from the past, they would not meet [him] now either; hence these three grades are not without a remote cause. The upper-birth one merely commits transgressions at random, knowing no shame. What the middle-birth one describes is mostly the five assemblies of renouncers who covet fame and profit and break the precepts. The lower-birth one commits the ten evil acts, the five grave offenses, and all the exceedingly heavy crimes. Since the crimes are light or heavy, they are divided into three classes.’
Gui 1: The lower-grade upper-birth

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “The upper-birth of the lower grade: If there are sentient beings who do many evil acts — though they do not slander the Vaipulya scriptures — such foolish people commit many evil dharmas and know no shame. When their life is about to end, they meet a good spiritual friend who explains to them the titles of the twelve sections of the Mahāyāna scriptures. Because they hear such [scriptural] names, they remove the exceedingly heavy evil karma of a thousand kalpas. The wise friend further teaches them to place their palms together and invoke ‘Namo Amitabha Buddha’; by invoking the Buddha’s name, they remove the karma of birth-and-death for five billion kalpas. At that time that Buddha sends a transformation-Buddha, a transformation-Avalokiteshvara, and a transformation-Mahasthamaprapta to come before that practitioner, who praises him: ‘Good man! Because you invoked the Buddha’s name, all your offenses are destroyed; I have come to welcome you!’ Having spoken these words, the practitioner sees the light of the transformation-Buddha filling his whole room. Seeing it, he is overjoyed and passes away at once. Riding on a jeweled lotus, he follows behind the transformation-Buddha and is born in the jeweled pond. After seven sevens (forty-nine days), the lotus unfolds. When the flower opens, the great compassionate Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva emit great light and stand before him, preaching the profound twelve sections of the scriptures. Having heard them and understood, he arouses the unsurpassed bodhi-mind. After ten small kalpas he perfects the hundred dharma-gates of illumination and enters the first stage. This is the upper-birth of the lower grade.”

The Shi-lun Commentary says: ‘The upper-birth ones of this grade are ordinary and [non-Buddhist] people who commit comparatively lighter offenses, and it is only at the end of life that they happen upon the opportunity to be told the names of the twelve Mahāyāna sections. This is by no means an easy matter. In China, where the Buddha’s instruction has flourished most, although Buddhist followers are many, those who know the names and meanings of all twelve divisions of the teaching are still rarely met. How much more [difficult] when this evil person, in the haste of death, encounters them by chance — unless his good roots from former lives happened to ripen at just this moment, how could he gain such a fortunate encounter? Even if someone could explain [the scriptures] in detail, in his pain and bewilderment he would hardly be able to listen attentively. Hence it is said that this matter is by no means easy. Hearing the scripture names and removing the heavy offenses of a thousand kalpas is already a fortunate matter; but compared with invoking the Buddha’s name, which removes the karma of birth-and-death for five million kalpas, the difference is still great. Moreover, invoking the Buddha’s name is simple, easy to practice, and the mind becomes concentrated; but as for hearing the scripture names, since he does not understand them they do not enter [his mind] and are rejected, so the efficacy is inferior. To get a person to explain the scripture names, though one may find such a person, is something one can meet but cannot seek; whereas to teach the invoking of the Buddha’s name — everyone can do it well. Some among the heterodox missionaries, when a convicted criminal is about to suffer the death penalty, take the opportunity to explain taking refuge to him; that is an excellent plan, and Buddhists too should adopt this method.’
Gui 2: The lower-grade middle-birth

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “The middle-birth of the lower grade: If there are sentient beings who transgress against the five precepts, the eight precepts, and the full precepts — such foolish people steal the property of the Saṃgha and the property of the Saṃgha present before them; they preach the Dharma impurely and know no shame. They adorn themselves with all their evil karma. Such offenders, because of evil karma, should fall into hell. When their life is about to end, the manifold fires of hell come together all at once. They meet a good spiritual friend, who, with great compassion, at once praises the ten powers and awesome virtues of Amitabha Buddha, extols at length the light and the spiritual power of that Buddha, and also praises precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge-and-vision of liberation. Having heard this, they remove the karma of birth-and-death for eight billion kalpas. The fierce fires of hell turn into a cool breeze, blowing heavenly flowers. On every flower are transformation-Buddhas and bodhisattvas, welcoming this person. In a single thought-moment he is reborn within a lotus in the pond of the seven jewels. After six kalpas the lotus unfolds. Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, with brahmic-voiced sounds, comfort that person and preach to him the profound scriptures of the Great Vehicle. Having heard this Dharma, he at once arouses the unsurpassed bodhi-mind. This is the middle-birth of the lower grade.”

The Yanyi commentary says: ‘The practitioners of this grade are of two kinds, monastic and lay: lay people may transgress the five and eight precepts, while bhikṣus may violate the great full precepts (the Ling-zhi Commentary says: “the text omits the novice’s precepts”). These two kinds are all unwise fools.’ The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘The property of the Saṃgha is the heaviest [to steal], hence it is singled out. ‘Saṃgha’ is here rendered ‘great assembly’ — that is, the perpetual property. Of this there are two kinds. First, the ‘perpetual, perpetual’ — the monastery buildings, grain, and rice, and so on. (The Miao-zong Commentary says: “First, the ‘perpetual, perpetual,’ meaning the monks’ kitchen and storehouse, the monastery halls and furnishings, flowers, fruits, trees, fields, gardens, servants, and cattle, and so on; because their substance is common to the ten directions, they cannot be divided up.”) Second, the ‘ten-direction perpetual’ — the food and drink offered to the monks, and so on. (The Miao-zong Commentary says: “Second, the ‘ten-direction perpetual,’ such as the monks’ ordinary meals offered to the Saṃgha; their substance is common to the ten directions, being limited only to the present place.”) The property of the Saṃgha present-before [one] is also of two kinds. First, the ‘present, present’ — what is divided according to the count. (As today’s lay people give to the monks of that place clothing, medicine, rooms, and utensils, etc. — see the Lecture Record of the Precepts.) Second, the ‘ten-direction present’ — what is broadly given with a communal intention. (As when the Saṃgha receives a gift, and the belongings of deceased [monks].) To steal any of these four kinds of Saṃgha property forms an offense. The Sūtra says: ‘The five grave offenses and the four heavy [offenses] I am still able to save; but one who steals the property of the Saṃgha I do not save.’ This is an extreme warning! The ‘impure preaching’ means borrowing the Buddha’s Dharma to seek gain and support. ‘Knowing no shame’ means openly doing [evil], within having no sense of shame. When evil traces are full to overflowing, it is therefore called ‘adorned [with them].’ ‘Should fall into hell’ — ‘should’ still means ‘necessarily.’ The manifold fires of hell are the cauldron of boiling water, the furnace of coals, molten copper, iron pellets, and so on. In [the description of] meeting the good friend, the merits of the Buddha spoken of are three: first, the ten powers; second, the light; third, the fivefold body of the Dharma. Hearing the Dharma extinguishes offenses, and the saints are moved to come and welcome; because he hears the Buddha’s virtues and in a single thought believes and accepts, he turns evil into good and the fire changes into a cool breeze. The world changes with the mind — its swiftness is like this!’

The Shi-lun Commentary says: ‘The middle-birth of the lower grade is [for] those who, being already followers of the Buddha, commit evil karma and add to it the offense of breaking the precepts, and moreover steal the common property of the Perpetual [Saṃgha] and the private property of the Saṃgha — this is to injure the [precious] Saṃgha. To preach the Dharma impurely is to confuse the [precious] Dharma. Fortunately, through good roots from former lives, at the end of life they hear the Buddha-Dharma extensively and can remove the karma of birth-and-death for eight billion kalpas. Yet because their offenses are comparatively heavy, they must be shut within the lotus for six kalpas. The Sūtra does not state the measure of the kalpa. According to [a reckoning] one small kalpa is 16,800,000 years, a middle kalpa is 336,000,000 years, and a great kalpa is 1,344,000,000 years. Thus a small kalpa is sixteen million years — how much more a middle or a great kalpa. This is not a punishment imposed by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, but the offender’s own karma forming the obstacle. The world should realize: heavy offenses must never be committed, and the Pure Land too does not depart from the law of cause and effect. What the Buddhas and bodhisattvas can save people from is [only] their not falling into evil destinies. To be nurtured for a long time within the flower-bud — this is, amidst misfortune, a great good fortune. The difference between the lotus-womb and hell is: first, the lotus-womb has no suffering while hell has extreme suffering; second, the opening of the flower has a fixed time whereas there is no time to escape from the Avīci hell. Unless one is utterly foolish, one should know what to choose and what to reject!’
Gui 3: The lower-grade lower-birth
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “The lower-birth of the lower grade:

The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘Among the headings, the upper and middle classes mark “the Buddha told [Ānanda and Vaidehī]” and so on only at the upper grade; only the three grades of the lower class each mark it one by one, because evil-doing [leading to] rebirth is contrary to the norm and startles the assembly — it is easily doubted and hard to believe — so the text repeatedly marks it, intending to make them listen and accept.’

If there are sentient beings who do unwholesome karmic deeds — the five grave offenses, the ten evil acts, with all unwholesome [deeds] complete — such foolish people, because of evil karma, should fall into the evil destinies, pass through many kalpas, and suffer without end.

In the explanation, first, the evil done in life. As for the five grave offenses: killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and drawing blood from the Buddha’s body. Violating and betraying debts of kindness, they are called the ‘five grave offenses.’ The retribution in this very life is to fall into Avīci [hell], so they are called the ‘five uninterrupted karmic deeds.’ The ten evil acts are the three of body, the four of speech, and the three of mind; all evil karma is gathered up in the ten. Having done the extremely heavy, nothing else goes undone — hence it says ‘all unwholesome [deeds are] complete.’ Question: The Larger Sūtra says: ‘Even [down] to ten thoughts, if they are not born in my land, I will not attain right enlightenment — only [those who commit] the five grave offenses and slander the right Dharma are excluded.’ Here the Sūtra [says] that even those [who commit] the five grave offenses can be reborn? Now [we] explain: If one relies on the power of Amitabha’s vows, how could it bar those who have committed offenses? Expediently responding to their capacities, the words differ but the purport accords. That [text] reveals the transcendent wonder of the Blissful Land, wishing to draw forward the good person; this [text] shows that the merit of the pure karma is deep and does not abandon even the extremely evil. So long as one holds the name and dedicates the vow, there is none whose offenses are not extinguished and who is not reborn. Hence the Sūtra of the Buddha-Contemplation Samādhi says: ‘The four assemblies [of disciples] who slander the Vaipulya scriptures, commit the five grave offenses, and violate the four grave prohibitions — if such people are able, with utmost sincerity for one day and one night, with sustained mindfulness to contemplate a single auspicious mark of the Buddha, all their evil offenses and hindrances are entirely extinguished.’ Citing that to prove this — that the offenses are extinguished, what is there to doubt? Below, [the text] shows the retribution to come. Upon committing a single grave offense, [one is in] Avīci for a kalpa; how much more for committing many — hence [the text] says ‘many kalpas.’ (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)

The Shi-lun Commentary says: ‘The lower-birth of the lower grade is [for] the extremely evil kind, whose deeds are the five uninterrupted karmic deeds — also commonly known in the world. Yet there are [offenses] that the world overlooks and easily commits: seducing and defiling monks and nuns, or not doing it oneself but causing others to do it — such as actors performing on the stage, and vulgar literati writing novels and chanted tales, treating [these] as elegant and amorous romances; this defiles the Buddhist gate and ruins the pure conduct of others, and also belongs to the karma of the uninterrupted hell. Let the foolish not bring sorrow upon themselves!’

Such a foolish person, at the end of life, meets a good spiritual friend who consoles him in every way, teaches him the wonderful Dharma, and instructs him to recite the Buddha. That person, pressed by suffering, has no leisure to [contemplate] the Buddha. The good friend says to him: ‘If you cannot contemplate that Buddha, you should invoke [his name:] Amitāyus Buddha.’ Thus, with utmost sincerity, he lets the sound never cease, and completes ten thoughts, invoking ‘Namo Amitabha Buddha.’
